messages.subject: Re: songbird data with questions on adjustment selection and
parts:
Hi Sandy,

> >I am using distance to analyze transects to determine avian abundance
> >(analyzed in clusters) in agricultural fields. I have tried multiple
> >truncations, groupings, and models and have come up with 'best' models for
> >each treatment/time period. I originally used the default 'sequential' for
> >adjustment terms and 'estimate variance empirically' for variance. Should
> >I go back and try the 'forward' adjustment selection

If you have "good" distance data (ie wide shoulder, smooth decline in
detection function) then it is unlikely to make much, if any difference. In
theory 'forward' adjustment selection is more flexible than sequential
selection of adjustment terms, as it tests all potential adjustment terms to
see which is "best" to add next. In fact, I'm not sure why this isn't the
default in Distance! -- I guess because (a) it is computationally more
intensive and (b) generally, for "good" data, you won't want/need to fit
high-order adjustment terms. Maybe one of the other distance sampling gurus
can shed some light on this? Anyway, as I said, it shouldn't make much
difference.

> > and bootstrap for variance? I know Distance Sampling (pg120) recommends
> >valuating the bootstrap on the final model, but is this always a superior
> >method of estimating variance? I have noticed, for the few that I have
> >already tried, that the CV for bootstrap is higher than the CV for the
> >analytical. Is this normal? Thanks for the help.

It is superior in that it makes fewer assumptions, and admits more real
sources of uncertainty.

For fewer assumptions: you don't use the analytic variance estimate of f(0),
so you are not relying on the assumption that observations are independant
(although this assumptions still plays a role in selection of adjustment
terms). If you use the percentile-based confidence limits you are also not
making any assumption about the distribution of the density estimate (the
parametric confidence limits assume it is log-normally distributed).

For more uncertainty, you are including the uncertainty due to selecting
adjustment terms. You can also put in more than one key function (Model
Definition | Detection Function | Models, + button) to include uncertainty
due to selecting which key function to use. You will end up with wider
confidence limits, but they will more accurately reflect your true
uncertainty. For more on model selection uncertainty, see:

Buckland, Burnham and Augustin. 1997. Model Selection: An Integral Part of
Inference. Biometrics 53: 603-618.

and part of

Burnham and Anderson. 1998. Model Selection and Inference. Springer Verlag.

One time that bootstrapping is a bad idea is when you only have a small
number of points or lines to bootstrap. Ideally you want at least 15-20
points or lines before you consider using bootstrapping -- otherwise your
results will likely be quite unreliable. This also applies to using points
or lines to give an empirical estimate of encounter rate variance.

Hope this helps,

- Len Thomas
